---
title: "Quiz: nearest neighbours and empty space"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What is $G(r)$, in one sentence? What is its value under CSR?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A cumulative histogram.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The fraction of points whose nearest neighbour is within distance r (the cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances). Under CSR $G(r) = 1 - e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$.
:::

---

**Q2.** How do G and F differ? For a clustered pattern, which one lies above the CSR curve?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
G starts at a point, F at a random location.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
G measures distances from each point to its nearest other point; F measures distances from random locations to the nearest point. In a clustered pattern points have close neighbours (G above CSR), while random locations often fall in big gaps (F below CSR).
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does J(r) need no estimate of the intensity?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is J for CSR, whatever ρ is?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Under CSR $1 - G = 1 - F = e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$, so their ratio is exactly 1 for every ρ. The reference line is the constant 1; no ρ enters.
:::

---

**Q4.** All points come in tight pairs 2 µm apart; the pairs are placed at random. Sketch G. What can G not tell you about this pattern?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Only the nearest neighbour counts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
G is 0 below 2 µm and jumps to 1 at 2 µm. It says nothing about larger distances: whether the pairs are random, clustered or regular at 20 µm is invisible to G (but not to K).
:::

---

**Q5.** Without a correction, is Ĝ near the border too high or too low? Does the pattern then look clustered or regular?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Some true neighbours are outside the window.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Neighbours outside the window are missed, so observed nearest distances are too long and Ĝ is too low: the pattern looks more regular than it is.
:::

---

**Q6.** In which of these is the edge effect largest: (a) 500 cells in a 1 × 1 mm square, (b) 30 cells in a 60 × 60 µm crop, (c) 100 cells along a 20 µm wide strip of epithelium?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What share of the points is within r of the border?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(c), then (b). In the narrow strip almost every point is close to the border; in a small crop many are; in a large square few are.
:::

---

**Q7.** The border rule makes Ĝ unbiased. What does it cost?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which points are used at large r?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Points closer to the border than r are left out, so at large r few points remain and Ĝ becomes noisy (and need not be monotone). In a thin strip it may leave no point at all.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the mean nearest-neighbour distance under CSR is $1/(2\sqrt\rho)$. With ρ = 0.01 µm⁻², what is it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$E[D] = \int_0^\infty P(D > r)\,dr$ and $\int_0^\infty e^{-ar^2}dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi/a}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P(D > r) = e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$, so $E[D] = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi/(\rho\pi)} = 1/(2\sqrt\rho)$. With ρ = 0.01: 5 µm.
:::
